questions.question_text: Write the normalised floating-point representation of the following positive binary number using this system (12-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent, two's complement): 0.00000001110101101
questions.mark_scheme:
MP1: Correct mantissa: 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 0
MP2: Correct exponent: 1 0 0 1
(Mantissa: 011101011010, Exponent: 1001)
The binary point is moved 8 places right so exponent = -7 in two's complement... wait, the number is 0.00000001110101101, normalised form is 0.1110101101... moving point 8 places right gives exponent of -8? No: normalised positive mantissa starts 0.1... The number 0.00000001110101101 needs the point moved 8 places right to get 0.111010110... so exponent = -8? Actually the number is shifted: 0.00000001110101101 → 0.1110101101 (shift 7 places left... no). Correct answer per mark scheme: Mantissa: 011101011010, Exponent: 1001 (which is -7 in two's complement... 1001 = -8+1 = -7). The binary point moves 7 places. Final answer: Mantissa: 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 0 | Exponent: 1 0 0 1
common_mistakes: Not normalising correctly (mantissa not starting with 01)
Incorrect exponent calculation
Forgetting two's complement for negative exponent
Truncating or rounding mantissa incorrectly

questions.question_text: Calculate the normalised binary floating-point representation of -76.1875 in this system (12-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent, two's complement). Show your working.
questions.mark_scheme:
MP1: Correct method to find the binary number e.g. 76.1875 = 64+8+4+0.125+0.0625 → 01001100.0011
MP2: Additional working towards binary number e.g. -76.1875 two's complement: 10110011.1101
MP3: Correct use of exponent - movement of binary point by 7 places // 1.011001111 01 × 2^7, exponent = 0111
MP4: Correct answer: Mantissa: 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 1 | Exponent: 0 1 1 1
common_mistakes: Not converting to two's complement for negative number
Incorrect normalisation (not starting with 10 for negative)
Wrong exponent value
Arithmetic errors in binary conversion of 76.1875

questions.question_text: Describe two ways in which packet switching ensures a complete message is received when passing messages across a network.
questions.mark_scheme:
Two marks for each description (2 x 2, Max 4):
1. Packets checked at receiving end / on arrival [1] … if packets arrive damaged or don't arrive at all, a re-send request is sent [1]
2. Packets routed through different paths / sent individually [1] … if a route is blocked, the packet is sent through a different route to ensure it arrives [1]
3. If the packet's hop count is exceeded [1] … the packet will be retired, which can generate a re-send request [1]
common_mistakes: Only giving one mark point per way without explaining the mechanism
Describing packet switching in general rather than specifically how it ensures completeness
Confusing packet switching with circuit switching

questions.question_text: Describe two ways in which the complexities of the computer hardware are hidden from the user.
questions.mark_scheme:
One mark for identification and one mark for a description (Max 4). Two from:
1. Provision of a User Interface // Provision of a Graphical User Interface [1] - Allows the user to interact with the computer in a more intuitive way // Icons and menus are used to control devices by simply 'pointing and clicking' [1]
2. Use of device drivers [1] - Makes it easier to control peripherals such as printers within the operating system rather than on the separate device itself [1]
3. Device mapping [1] - Different devices (physical and virtual) are easy to identify on the network, check their status, or use [1]
4. The user interacts only with the Application / top layer (of the TCP/IP protocol suite) [1] - leaving the lower layers and their complexities hidden from the user [1]
common_mistakes: Identifying a way without describing it
Vague descriptions that don't explain how complexity is hidden
Repeating the same idea in different words for both ways

questions.question_text: Complete the pseudocode for the function to remove a data item from the stack.
questions.mark_scheme:
One mark for each correctly completed line (Max 5):
FUNCTION Pop() RETURNS STRING
DECLARE DataItem : STRING
DataItem ← ""
IF Top > –1 // Top >= Base THEN
  DataItem ← StackArray[Top]
  Top ← Top – 1
ELSE
  DataItem ← "You cannot remove data; the stack is empty"
ENDIF
RETURN DataItem // StackArray[Top + 1]
ENDFUNCTION
common_mistakes: Wrong condition for checking empty stack (e.g. Top == -1 instead of Top > -1)
Not decrementing Top after removal
Returning wrong value
Missing RETURNS STRING in function header
Accessing wrong index in array
